lesson.title: Survival of the Fitted: How Natural Selection Actually Works
lesson.summary: This section explains natural selection, the mechanism Charles Darwin proposed to account for how species change over generations, and shows how this same mechanism underlies the evolutionary perspective on behavior.
lesson.body:
Natural selection is the mechanism, first clearly described by Charles Darwin, that explains how species gradually change over many generations. The process rests on a few straightforward ingredients. First, individuals within a population vary in their traits, no two members of a species are exactly identical. Second, at least some of that variation is heritable, meaning it can be passed from parents to offspring through genes. Third, in any given environment, some variants help the individuals who carry them survive and reproduce more successfully than individuals with other variants, a difference researchers call differential reproductive success. Put these three ingredients together across many generations, and traits linked to greater reproductive success gradually become more common in the population, while traits linked to lower reproductive success gradually become rarer.

A common misunderstanding is worth correcting directly. Natural selection is not survival of the strongest, and it does not involve any intention, goal, or effort on the part of the organism. No individual animal or person decides to evolve a helpful trait. Natural selection is a passive filtering process: whichever heritable variants happen to help their carriers leave more surviving offspring in a particular environment simply become more common over time, purely as a statistical consequence of unequal reproduction, not because anything or anyone planned it that way.

A well documented example from outside psychology helps make the mechanism concrete. In regions where industrial pollution darkened the bark of trees, a species of moth that came in both light and dark colorings shifted noticeably toward the dark coloring over time. Before the pollution, light colored moths blended in better against light bark and were less often spotted and eaten by birds, so they had the survival advantage. Once pollution darkened the bark, dark colored moths blended in better instead, gaining the same kind of advantage the light colored moths had previously held, and the population's balance of colors shifted accordingly across generations. Nothing about the moths themselves changed, what changed was which existing variant the environment now favored.

Natural selection is the actual engine behind the evolutionary perspective on behavior described in the previous section. Over vast stretches of time, this same filtering process is what could take a heritable behavioral tendency, such as a predisposition toward quickly learned caution around ancestral dangers, and gradually make it widespread across an entire species, rather than something that appears only randomly in scattered individuals.

It is worth remembering that natural selection operates on populations across many generations, not on individuals across a single lifetime. It can help explain why a tendency is widespread across humans as a species, but it cannot explain why any one particular person behaves a certain way on any one particular day, that gap is exactly where individual genetic differences, discussed in the heredity and behavior sections, and personal environment and experience continue to matter.
